meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Strength does not come from physical capacity'?
meta.ogDescription: Universally credited to Mahatma Gandhi. The sentiment is genuinely his — the exact sentence has no source we could verify.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1869–1948 · Indian independence leader & apostle of nonviolence
answer.sourceLine: Credited to Gandhi by every quotation site that carries it, and the thought is squarely his — satyagraha is an argument that will beats force. But the exact sentence could not be tied to a primary text. The one citation in circulation, a bare reference to Young India (1919) on the Wikiquote talk page, gives no article, date or page, and could not be checked against the paper itself.

source.trailTitle: What we could and could not establish
trail: The line appears on Wikiquote’s Gandhi page ↗; the only sourcing offered anywhere in that page’s history is a note on its talk page ↗ pointing at Young India, volume 1, issue 52, 1919 — a citation with no article title, date or page number.

Young India is real: Gandhi’s English-language weekly, which he wrote for and edited from 1919 to 1931. Scanned runs are on the Internet Archive ↗, so the citation is checkable in principle. It was not checkable from this session.

Every other source that carries the line — BrainyQuote, Goodreads, AZ Quotes, passiton and the rest — prints it with no citation at all. That pattern, a clean epigram with universal credit and no primary text behind it, is the standard profile of a paraphrase that hardened into a quotation.
No source was found that refutes Gandhi’s authorship either. This is an unproven attribution, not a debunked one.
source.excerptNote: A shortened form, ‘Strength does not come from physical capacity but from an indomitable will,’ circulates alongside the two-sentence version. Neither has a located source, and the drift between them is itself weak evidence that the wording was smoothed in transmission.
source.rightsNote: Rights cannot be settled, because the source cannot be. If the line really is from Young India in 1919 it would be comfortably public domain in the United States, where the threshold is publication before 1931. But that date is exactly the thing this page could not confirm, so no public-domain claim is made here. Treat the sentence as quoted for identification only.

author.name: Mahatma Gandhi
author.heading: About Mahatma Gandhi
author.metaLine: 1869–1948 · Indian independence leader & apostle of nonviolence
author.bio: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi led India’s independence movement through satyagraha — nonviolent civil resistance — and made a political method out of the claim that moral force outlasts physical force. He wrote constantly: his Collected Works run to roughly a hundred volumes, and he edited the weekly Young India for twelve years. That is why an unsourced Gandhi line is worth flagging rather than assuming. With a paper trail that large, a sentence that cannot be found in it is a sentence worth doubting — even when it sounds exactly like him.

misattribution.heading: The catch: an unproven source, not a wrong author
misattribution.intro: Nobody has shown this line belongs to someone else. What nobody has shown is where Gandhi wrote it — and with a hundred volumes of collected works to search, that absence is worth stating plainly rather than papering over.

items.why: The sentence is polished in a way Gandhi’s journalism generally is not, and it circulates in two forms — the two-sentence version and a compressed ‘but from an indomitable will.’ Wording that drifts is wording that was passed along, not read off a page.

‘Young India, volume 1, issue 52, 1919’ names no article, no date and no page. It is the sort of reference that comes from a catalogue record rather than from reading the issue, and it could not be checked against the scanned run.

misattribution.truthLine: The idea is authentically Gandhian and no one has produced a rival author — but the sentence has no source we could verify, so this page calls it attributed rather than verified.

context.heading: Why it sounds so much like Gandhi
lead: The line reads as pure Gandhi because it compresses his central political wager. Satyagraha — literally ‘holding firmly to truth’ — was built on the claim that a disciplined will, willing to absorb violence without returning it, would outlast an empire with all the physical capacity. He was a slight man who fasted as a tactic; the contrast between bodily weakness and moral force was not a metaphor to him but a method.

That is also why the attribution has stuck so hard without a source. The sentence does not misrepresent him. It just has not been shown to be his sentence, and on a site whose whole point is the difference between those two things, that distinction is the story.
context.detailsSummary: What it would take to settle this
detailsBody: The claim is checkable. Young India for 1919 to 1922 is scanned and public on the Internet Archive, and the Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi are searchable. A reader who finds the sentence — or establishes that it is a translator’s or biographer’s rendering of a longer passage — would move this page from attributed to verified, or to disputed.
Until then the honest position is the uncomfortable one: universally credited, entirely in character, and unsourced.
context.pull: A hundred volumes of collected works, and the sentence is in none of them that we could find.
